<reason>Side B dismantled Side A's case by exposing the practical and legal flaws of regulating unpredictable third-party behavior like a static physical defect. Side B proved that triggering disclosures from management logs penalizes conscientious landlords while rewarding negligent ones who keep no records, and that liability fears would simply produce universal boilerplate disclaimers that weaken tenants' post-move-in quiet enjoyment claims. Worse, Side A fatally confused the comparative baseline in both Pressure Questions [A3.1] and Closing [A5.2], arguing that under Side B's regime diligent landlords get punished with a "scarlet letter" while slumlords face no disclosure duty—accidentally conceding Side B's central indictment of the proposition itself.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B2.1]-[B2.2] and [B5.1], Side B turned Side A's own definition of the disclosure trigger ("documented patterns in management logs") against the motion, showing it punishes proactive landlords who log complaints while letting slumlords evade the rule by taking only verbal reports—a point Side A accidentally conceded in [A5.2].</best_rebuttal>
